For our primary chart, we created a bar chart to compare the Virginia counties across our three main statistics (number of severe accidents, severe ratio, and severe rate). This chart serves as a general summary comparison across different Virginia counties. The channel we used was length of a bar to carry this key comparison. One graph we considered for this key comparison is a violin plot to compare counties, but we rejected it because violin plots are used to compare the spread of data from its median whereas if a governor is sourcing resources to help different counties with their accident rates, they would be more concerned about the means of each county.

Our dashboard primarily uses 95% confidence intervals to display uncertainty. These are used to compare county group means on monthly severe accident rates and monthly severe accident ratios. For example, a viewer looking at the counties with the top 5 populations can say I am 95% confident, for Prince William County, Fairfax County, and Virginia Beach County, that the mean true severe rate rests between 30-50%. The purpose of these Confidence Intervals is to provide the governor a sense of, on an average month, what is the severe rate or ratio for each county likely to be and how does this county compare to other counties in a similar condition (high population for example). Furthermore, our dashboard includes confidence intervals for weather conditions. This looked at the question, which weather condition is most strongly associated with accidents that are severe. Higher valued confidence intervals suggest that this specific weather condition is more likely to be active when a severe accident takes place.

Our dashboard omits prediction intervals. For a resource decision about where to source different resources to meet the worst cases of accident load, what is important to the decision is how county groupings are different from each other. This question calls for a Confidence Interval comparing different means. A prediction interval instead would answer the question of what the next severe rate or ratio is expected to be in that county which is less useful for making a governing decision about where to source resources to help with accidents.

Colors chosen in our dashboard are primarily on the color scale using blues, red, and yellows. This primarily helps individuals with red/green color blindness, as green colors are not in the dashboard. Each dashboard image also carries an accessibility screen reader alternative caption so that someone who relies on a screen reader can understand the image they are looking at. Finally, there is a method in the dashboard to click a button and download a summary excel document. This document provides summary statistics for the top 5 counties and include the following statistics: number of total accidents, number of severe accidents, severe rate, severe ratio, months observed, mean monthly total accidents, mean monthly severe accidents, mean monthly severe ratio, mean monthly severe rate and their respective confidence intervals. The Excel provided is dynamic based on year, so a colorblind viewer could download summaries for just one year only (2016) or the full span of data (2016-2023). Finally, on the hotspot map, color carries a statistic, severe rate, which is an intensive quantity. This rate is not biased by the amount of population in a county.

After interviewing three people, we received positive but differing reactions to the dashboard. Person A generally found it more straightforward and not too cluttered. Additionally, they thought the second page was easier to understand and felt the third page was the most effective for visualizing where the crashes in Virginia occurred. Person B felt that the summary page (page 1) contained too much information. For a summary page, they were expecting one main graph to summarize across different populations and received three graphs instead with different varying drop downs to change the view. They had difficulty interpreting the summary graphs and confidence interval graphs due to some unfamiliarity with the Statistics terms themselves. For example, they interpreted the confidence interval graph on the summary page as box plots. This finding was also supported by our interview with person C who had no idea what a Confidence Interval is and felt that the dashboard contained too many jargon heavy labels. Person A and Person B agreed that the county filter and chart labels were the most valuable dashboard features. At the end of the interview, Person A and Person B identified the top five counties in population as having the highest frequency of severe traffic accidents and referred to the weather conditions on the first page as most strongly associated with them.

However, Person C suggested that these chart labels should also be enabled by default on each graph instead of relying on hovering over the bar for them to pop out and felt that the filter for confidence intervals was unclear because it was not placed near the graph itself. They also suggested that the large banner on page 1 with summary statistics for accidents, severe accident rate, and severe accident ratio made the summary page too busy and were not helpful because they didn't compare anything. Furthermore, he felt that if our question is focused on which five Virginia counties experience the highest frequency of severe accidents, page 2 and page 3 where interesting but not informative in a way that mattered for the specific question. Finally, he additionally identified a bug in the graph where you could zoom in on a graph but had no ability to zoom back out unless you double clicked on the graph itself. This was because the individual plotly graphs did not show their navigation buttons.

Overall, all participants felt that the information on Page 1 was too detailed and jargon heavy to serve as an effective summary page. Based on their responses, some charts from the first page of the dashboard could be moved or removed so that the first page provides a better overall summary. Furthermore, some visualizations could be simplified or better labeled to make the findings easier to interpret specifically for individuals who may not be familiar with specific statistics' terminology like Confidence Intervals, Binomial, Poisson, etc. For example, the screen reader text summary could be expanded to provide more information as to what a confidence interval is or a separate data dictionary could be provided to expand on these Statistics terms. The confidence interval graphs and separate data table could also be incorporated as an optional selection for the viewer where if a viewer wants to understand the uncertainty around our primary chart, they can click a button that opens a new screen or page with the confidence intervals comparing each county. Going forward for M4 and the final presentation, we will consider making these changes on the dashboard.

Finally, we should spend some time rethinking our question from M1. The question was:

\begin{quote}\noindent\textit{Which five Virginia counties experience the highest frequency of severe traffic accidents, and which weather conditions are most strongly related to these severe accidents?}\end{quote}

\noindent Specifically, if we are going to show Page 2 which shows specific information on a single county and Page 3 which shows a map of Virginia, what parts of our original question do these help answer if any, and if not does our question need to be rephrased. For example, we could change the word counties to the word localities so that the question allows us to consider cities, and narrow the second part of the question to refer to the weather conditions within each locality.
